articles.title: Teen’s life changed by gene editing that stopped blood disorder symptoms
articles.summary: Vian, 16, has thalassemia and had to have monthly blood transfusions throughout her childhood.
articles.body:
A teenager has revealed how her life has been transformed thanks to pioneering gene editing, which reversed symptoms of a crippling blood disorder.

Vian, 16, was born with thalassemia, a condition that affects haemoglobin - used by red blood cells to transport oxygen around the body. It left her short of breath and with no appetite.

Her own stem cells were edited and she no longer needs the monthly blood transfusions she endured for most of her life.

"My whole life's different now. It's changed so much," she said.

The treatment, for patients with thalassaemia or sickle cell disease, is offered to young people at three children's hospitals in the country.

Vian, from Coventry, was one of the first to have it.

Her edited stem cells were returned to her last December, following chemotherapy, and she has now recovered well.

"It's much easier for me now. I always have energy to do stuff," Vian explained.

"I'm like, ‘mum let's go out’. Before, I would just sleep, always tired."

She has started studying health and social care at college, with ambitions of becoming a nurse, having spent most of her life surrounded by medical staff.

"I have more options now. Before, I couldn't do most things other kids could," she added.

"I usually sat out of PE. I really love PE, but I couldn't do that."

Consultant haematologist Dr Sarah Lawson describes the treatment as a "functional cure" - the disease doesn't go away, but the aspects that caused problems are removed.

"We collect the stem cells. They are sent off to a manufacturing laboratory where they are edited...and that changes how those stem cells work and it makes them produce more foetal or baby haemoglobin," she said.

"And in a patient with thalassaemia, that allows them to be transfusion free, and [in] a patient with sickle cell disease, it gives them a high baby haemoglobin level, which then negates the problems with the sickle haemoglobin.

"When I was at medical school, which was a long time ago, I remember learning a little bit about gene therapy and it being talked about then. And for it now to be a reality 20-odd years later is incredible."

JoelSamuel, 14, from Oldbury, is at the start of his journey.

His sickle cell disease leaves him in excruciating pain.

Like thalassemia, the disease also involves red blood cells and is usually a lifelong condition, affecting patients' joints and leaving them feeling weak and tired.

JoelSamuel's stem cells have recently been collected at Birmingham Children's Hospital.

They will be edited and in six months he will have chemotherapy before his edited cells are returned to him.

He dreams of being able to enjoy sport. Attempts to do that now make him ill.

"I get tired and then the next day I get sick and I won't be able to go to school," he said.

He explained that he was initially nervous about having the treatment, but also feels hopeful.

"I think it's good to make me better, so I can go and do stuff that takes my energy," he said.

JoelSamuel has suffered a lot. His parents say they are praying the treatment will help him.

His father Alfred, who is 47 and runs a logistics company, said: "There are a few patients that have been on it, mainly with thalassemia instead of sickle cell. So we are hoping that we might get the same effects from it.

"Hopefully he might be able to play football after all."

JoelSamuel's mother Juliet, a 41-year-old seamstress, said: "I just can't wait to see him doing the normal things that everybody does at his age."

Vian has now been discharged from hospital.

We asked her if she had a message for JoelSamuel at the start of his treatment journey.

"Imagine all the things you can do while being healthy again.

"I think you can do it, I did it and so can you. I know it's going to be really hard and the trauma and everything, the nurses, the medicine, everything, but it's worth it."

articles.title: Woman given wrong blood after accident; hospital's unusual defence fails before consumer panel
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Chhattisgarh has directed a hospital and two doctors to pay Rs 5.1 lakh to a woman who was allegedly given
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Chhattisgarh has directed a hospital and two doctors to pay Rs 5.1 lakh to a woman who was allegedly given blood of the wrong group during treatment after an accident. The commission found that the woman had B-positive blood but was given AB-positive blood, causing her physical distress and putting her life at risk.The commission passed the order on September 29, 2026, holding the hospital and the two doctors responsible for deficiency in service and negligence. It directed them to pay Rs 5 lakh as compensation for mental agony and Rs 10,000 towards legal expenses within 45 days.What happened during the woman's treatment?As per the commission order, Madhu Khakha was returning to Raipur from Bilaspur with her daughter and other family members on February 16, 2014, when their car collided with a truck.Khakha suffered a fracture in her thigh bone and was taken to Balaji Institute of Medical Sciences in Raipur for treatment. She alleged that the hospital began treatment after Rs 25,000 was deposited at the time of admission.The next day, doctors ordered several tests, including a blood group test. The hospital's report identified her blood group as AB-positive, and arrangements were made for three units of AB-positive blood.However, Khakha alleged that she told the hospital staff that her blood group was B-positive. According to her complaint, the staff did not take her warning into account and proceeded with the transfusion.She further alleged that she began shivering soon after the blood transfusion started. Her condition worsened, and she began vomiting and lost consciousness. The blood supply was stopped, and she was given further treatment.The complaint also claimed that blood-like discharge appeared in her urine. The woman was later told that the wrong blood group had been transfused and that her fracture surgery would have to be postponed.Khakha and her family eventually decided to leave the hospital on February 24, 2014, and seek further treatment elsewhere because they had lost confidence in the hospital.Commission's findingThe bench of president Dakeshwar Prasad Sharma along with members Anil Kumar Agnihotri and Nirupama Pradhan examined the medical records, blood test reports and the hospital's defence. The hospital and doctors denied negligence, arguing that the woman had been admitted not only for a thigh fracture but also for other serious injuries suffered in the accident.They claimed that her condition was unstable and that medical complications during a state of shock could affect blood group testing. They also argued that the blood transfusion had been stopped after she developed a reaction.The commission, however, examined the blood test reports produced by both sides. It noted that the hospital's report dated February 17, 2014, recorded Khakha's blood group as AB-positive. A later report dated February 20 showed her blood group as B-positive.The commission also referred to a medical opinion sought from the civil surgeon-cum-chief hospital superintendent of the district hospital in Pandri. The expert was asked whether a person's blood group could change because of surrounding medical circumstances.The response was that a person's blood group could not change due to such circumstances. The commission therefore did not accept the hospital's explanation that the difference in blood group could be justified by the woman's condition.The commission also noted that Khakha had complained of shivering and other physical distress after the transfusion began, but the hospital staff had not paid adequate attention to her condition.The commission said that the woman's account showed that she had begun experiencing physical distress after the transfusion started, but the staff continued giving her blood despite her condition worsening.It further observed that the hospital's defence that only two to five drops of blood had been transfused before the reaction was not supported by the medical evidence placed before it. The commission noted that the hospital had not produced evidence to establish its explanation for the conflicting blood group results.“On examining the above questions and answers, the defence taken by the opposite parties cannot be accepted as medically justified. The expert has stated that a blood group cannot change due to surrounding circumstances,” the commission concluded.The commission held that Khakha had B-positive blood but was given AB-positive blood, resulting in physical and mental suffering. It said the hospital and doctors had shown serious negligence during her treatment.Khakha had sought Rs 19 lakh as compensation for mental agony and Rs 50,000 towards legal expenses. She had also sought the return of Rs 25,000 allegedly deposited when she was admitted to the hospital.The commission found that the claimed Rs 25,000 had not been supported by a bill, so it did not order its refund. It also considered the larger compensation claim excessive, but held that the woman had faced mental distress and a risk to her life because of the wrong blood transfusion.The commission observed that giving a patient blood of an incompatible group could lead to a serious, potentially fatal reaction if not treated promptly. It therefore held the hospital and doctors liable to compensate her.The commission's translated conclusion was that the opposite parties had provided AB-positive blood even though the woman's blood group was B-positive, amounting to deficiency in service and unfair conduct.Final orderThe District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Raipur, partly allowed Khakha's complaint and directed the hospital and two doctors to:Pay Rs 5 lakh as compensation for mental agony.Pay Rs 10,000 towards legal expenses.Make the payments within 45 days of the order.The compensation and legal expenses are payable jointly and severally by the opposite parties. The commission did not direct them to refund the Rs 25,000 admission payment because the woman had not produced a bill to prove that amount.The order holds the hospital and doctors responsible for negligence in the treatment, while limiting the compensation to the amounts the commission found justified by the material before it.

articles.title: McDonald's offers pickle juice to marathon runners, health experts question whether it works
articles.summary: A sports dietitian cautions against competitive runners trying pickle juice on race day. McDonald's will be distributing bottles along the Chicago Marathon route.
articles.body: McDonald's is putting its own briny twist on marathon weekend in Chicago. The fast-food giant is handing out limited-edition bottles of "Pickle Boost" to runners and spectators during Chicago Marathon weekend, starting Oct. 9 and continuing through race day on Oct. 11. McDonald's said the promotion is inspired by pickle juice's popularity among athletes who use it when muscle cramps strike during workouts. COMMON KITCHEN STAPLE MAY HELP RELIEVE MILD CONSTIPATION, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS Runners can pick up the bottles at a Friday morning pop-up on Chicago's Lakefront Trail, then at five McDonald's locations along or near the marathon route on race day, while supplies last. The promotion taps into a longstanding belief that pickle juice can help prevent muscle cramps, which science partially backs up. MCDONALD'S ROLLS OUT NEW 'PROTEIN' MENU BADGES, AND SOCIAL MEDIA USERS QUESTION THE NUMBERS "Pickle juice may help relieve muscle cramps, but the research is mixed," said Jena Brown, RD, CSSD, a Texas-based sports dietitian and owner of Victorem Performance Nutrition, which works with endurance athletes. One small study found that pickle juice appeared to help electrically induced cramps subside more quickly than water in dehydrated participants, said Brown, who is a longtime runner herself. But that research did not examine runners during an actual marathon, and another study found no benefit. "I would not recommend trying pickle brine for the first time on race day." "Muscle cramps are not fully understood and are likely not induced by a singular cause for all runners," she said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Electrolyte losses may contribute to cramps in some athletes, but pickle juice's possible benefit may not be as simple as replacing sodium, Brown said. Another theory is that vinegar may stimulate receptors in the mouth and gut and affect signaling between the nervous system and muscles. The evidence for that explanation is limited, and it should not turn pickle brine into a runner's primary race-day strategy, Brown said. "Pickle brine is not a replacement for a hydration and fueling plan," Brown said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES A typical sports drink supplies fluid and carbohydrates for energy, while a small sip of brine offers little fluid and no fuel, even though it contains electrolytes lost through sweat, she said. Runners who have tried pickle brine in training may tolerate it well and believe it helps, Brown said. But she cautioned against debuting the sour, salty remedy on the day of the marathon. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "I would not recommend trying pickle brine for the first time on race day," she said. If a severe cramp hits and a runner opts to try it, Brown recommends taking small sips rather than chugging it and gently stretching the affected muscle. Runners who are sensitive to salty or acidic drinks should be especially careful, she added, particularly later in a race when heat, fatigue and stomach upset can become bigger concerns. articles.title: Man loses 15 stubborn pounds after age 50 without giving up pizza or donuts
articles.summary: Carl Daikeler lost 15 pounds by swapping breakfast for a 250-calorie shake and eating a big salad for lunch, then enjoying total dinner freedom.
articles.body: Maintaining weight loss in midlife doesn’t necessarily require strict dietary bans or extreme fasting protocols. Carl Daikeler, co-founder and CEO of the fitness and nutrition company BODi, says a simple routine earlier in the day has helped him manage his weight while allowing more freedom at dinner. Los Angeles-based Daikeler, 63, who has led the health brand formerly known as Beachbody for 28 years, openly admits that he doesn't have an affinity for healthy foods. 10-MINUTE FITNESS HABIT CAN HELP ADULTS OVER 40 MAINTAIN MUSCLE AND STAY STRONG "I eat like a third-grader, okay? Pizza's a food group," Daikeler joked in an interview with Fox News Digital. "I'm just constantly trying to figure out how can I hack my way without having to overturn my life to become one of those diehard health and fitness people, because I'm never going to become that." When Daikeler turned 57, he found himself unable to lose 15 pounds he had gained around his waistline. Rather than adopting a strict diet, he adjusted two specific meals during the day while leaving his evening schedule unrestricted, he shared. For breakfast, Daikeler replaced standard options with a nutrient-dense shake containing protein, fiber, prebiotics, probiotics and greens, totaling roughly 250 calories. NIGHTLY GLASS OF WINE MAY NOT BE AS HARMLESS AS MANY PEOPLE THINK, STUDY SUGGESTS "I got rid of breakfast, or I changed my breakfast to this shake that we've got called Shakeology," Daikeler said. "I put some spinach in there and I put a banana in there." For lunch, Daikeler prepares a large salad loaded with baby spinach, carrots and chicken, mixed with toppings that mask the taste of the greens. "I hide it with some cheese, some nuts, some sliced strawberries, and it's delicious, and I put chicken in there ... I don't feel like I'm eating a bowl of vegetables, but I am." By keeping breakfast and lunch relatively structured, Daikeler gives himself more flexibility at dinner. BEER, WINE OR LIQUOR? MASSIVE STUDY REVEALS WHICH WAS LINKED TO LOWER DEATH RISK "Now I've got a 'day pass' for everything else ... I eat whatever I want at dinner." He does, however, follow a single guideline regarding alcohol intake. "I'm careful not to drink too much," he said. "Now I've got a 'day pass' for everything else ... I eat whatever I want at dinner." "Once I did that — Shakeology for breakfast, a big salad for lunch, total freedom for dinner, limited alcohol — the 15 pounds just got wiped out. And it stayed off." Daikeler warns that overly restrictive nutrition plans are usually difficult to stick with long-term, leading many to abandon their health goals entirely. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "If you're trying to be too restrictive, I don't think that's life," he said. "The whole point is living ... So if it's too restrictive, it's going to break." CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Instead of completely banning indulgence foods, Daikeler recommends using portion control and mindfulness to enjoy without overeating. "I love pizza. But I've learned that I can enjoy pizza without eating the whole pizza," he said. "I like doughnuts. I've learned that I can have literally a quarter of a doughnut and be like, that was delicious. But I get no additional satisfaction by eating the whole doughnut." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER For Daikeler, that balance is part of a broader focus on "health span" — prioritizing quality of life and the ability to stay active as he ages. "Health span versus lifespan is all about quality of life," he said. "I'm all for longevity, but it's really about quality of life — a way to live and enjoy life that is balanced with maximizing your time on earth." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP While Daikeler said this approach has worked for him, weight-loss strategies are not one-size-fits-all. According to the National Institutes of Health, different eating plans can support weight loss, but the most effective approach depends on a person's individual health needs, preferences and ability to maintain the habits long-term. Individuals are generally advised to consult a doctor or registered dietitian for personalized guidance.

articles.title: Why are more young women experiencing period problems?
articles.summary: Young women are more aware of menstrual complications and are relating issues like irregularity, pains, heavy bleeding, irregular cycles, weariness and
articles.body: Young women are more aware of menstrual complications and are relating issues like irregularity, pains, heavy bleeding, irregular cycles, weariness and mood changes. It is important to understand the difference between an increase of menstrual problems or merely getting better recognition and refer to the symptoms of such problems. There are menstrual health issues today due to the lifestyle of modern people, and the symptoms should not be ignored. Menstrual health is the result of a complicated interaction between hormones, nutrition, metabolism, the reproductive system and psychological stress.Key Reasons Behind Period ProblemsHormonal Imbalances and PCOSPolycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) is a prevalent disorder that leads to hormonal dysfunction resulting in menstrual irregularities in women with elevated androgen concentration. The hallmark features of PCOS are irregular or absent menstruation and possible presence of acne and hair growth in women. Hormonal disorders in PCOS may also contribute to insulin insensitivity in some, yet not all, of the patients.PCOS cannot be diagnosed simply based on an irregularity in cycles. The early stages of puberty are sometimes mistaken for PCOS, and therefore age-appropriate diagnostic standards must be used.Stress, Sleep and Energy ImbalanceThe HPO axis that produces reproductive hormones can be hampered by factors like chronic stress, inadequate caloric intake, excessive exercise, and rapid weight change. When the body has less reproductive hormone, symptoms include irregular ovulation and missed periods.Young women, who undergo high academic loads and hard work and need to follow a low-calorie diet, as well as undergo severe physical strain, may miss their periods one time or another. Yet, this reason should not be the only one for the missed periods.Painful Periods and EndometriosisA lot of young women face the issue of painful periods known in medicine as dysmenorrhea. Primary dysmenorrhea happens when prostaglandin levels in the body become too high. Prostaglandin is a chemical that contracts the uterus during this period of time and triggers inflammation.However, extreme cases of menstrual pain should not be ignored. Endometriosis is also an example of secondary dysmenorrhea that may affect teenagers. This condition occurs when tissues similar to the lining of the uterus develop in abnormal areas outside the uterus. If the pain affects a person’s daily life and causes problems while carrying out normal activities like going to school, work, and even sleeping, then it should be evaluated by an expert gynaecologist.Nutritional Deficiencies and Heavy BleedingMenorrhagia, which refers to excessive blood loss during menstruation, may result in iron deficiency, leading to the onset of anaemia, characterized by weakness, tiredness, and an inability to focus. At the same time, unhealthy eating habits may interfere with the hormonal balance and the period regularity.Taking iron supplements may be extremely dangerous for young females suffering from menorrhagia without identifying the underlying reason for the symptoms. The hormonal imbalance, absence of ovulation and some blood disorders may increase the risk of excess blood loss during menstruation.When Should a Woman Consult a Gynaecologist?It is crucial to evaluate the problems of menstruation in young females from the view of hormonal well-being, nutrition and lifestyle and try to understand whether any medications or substances have been taken in cases where menstruation is problematic, characterized by irregularities, heaviness or pain. If a woman doesn’t have her menstrual cycle for more than 90 days in a row in cases when the first menstrual cycle didn’t happen recently, she should go through medical evaluation. Next, it is important to state that severe pain may require further medical examination for possible diseases like endometriosis.Period problems in females should be seen as disorders originating from hormonal background, nutrition and lifestyle factors, but the problems may also depend on medications which were previously taken.(Dr Kajal Singh, Professor, Department of Gynaecology & Obstetrics, Noida International Institute of Medical Sciences (NIIMS), College & Hospital, Greater Noida)Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: 'Ozempic babies' are real — here's what doctors want you to know about fertility and GLP-1 drugs
articles.summary: Reproductive endocrinologists explain how these medications affect fertility and why some can make birth control pills less reliable.
articles.body:
Our experts independently review everything we recommend. If you buy through our links, we may earn commission.

"Ozempic babies" has become the internet's shorthand for surprise pregnancies among people taking GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy . Scroll TikTok and you'll find plenty of people sharing their positive pregnancy tests just months after starting one of these medications. The usual explanation is that GLP-1 drugs boost fertility, and for some people, they do help ovulation return. But fertility doctors point to a second factor that gets far less attention: tirzepatide, the drug in Mounjaro and Zepbound , can make birth control pills less effective, especially in the first weeks of treatment. If you're trying to get pregnant, that first part may sound like good news, but there are a couple of catches you need to know about. And if you're not trying to get pregnant, the second part is the one to watch. We asked four reproductive endocrinologists what's really going on and what to do about it.

Why Mounjaro and Zepbound can make the pill less reliable

Tirzepatide, the active ingredient in Mounjaro and Zepbound, "delays gastric emptying, particularly when treatment is first started," says reproductive endocrinologist Dr. Lucky Sekhon , an assistant clinical professor at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. "That can change the rate and extent at which an oral medication is absorbed." Put simply, birth control pills may be less effective, especially in the first few weeks.

In fact, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) labels for both Mounjaro and Zepbound state that after a single dose of tirzepatide, about 20% less of certain birth control hormones reached the bloodstream. That's why the labels advise switching to a non-oral contraceptive method, or adding a barrier method like condoms, for four weeks after starting tirzepatide and again after every dose increase. That second part catches people off guard, since doses go up "in steps every few weeks," says Dr. Deborah Ikhena-Abel , a reproductive endocrinologist in Austin.

Do Ozempic and Wegovy have the same effect?

Not as far as studies show. While semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, slows digestion too, it hasn't been shown to make the pill less effective, according to a 2026 review in JBRA Assisted Reproduction . "Medications within the GLP-1 family can have different pharmacokinetic effects," Sekhon says, "so we shouldn't assume that an interaction demonstrated with one drug automatically applies equally to another." That said, Foundayo , a newer daily GLP-1 pill , carries a precautionary backup warning on its label, though its effect on the pill hasn't been studied.

Still, some doctors, including Dr. Ilana Ressler , a reproductive endocrinologist at Illume Fertility in Norwalk, Conn., suggest "erring on the side of caution" and switching to a non-oral method or adding condoms with any GLP-1 drug, at least at first. Here's why:

Side effects can get in the way. Common GLP-1 drug side effects like vomiting and diarrhea can keep a pill from being fully absorbed.

Your ovulation may come back. "Patients whose ovulation improves during treatment may become pregnant sooner than they expect," Ressler says. (More on this below.)

Sekhon calls that "a precautionary, individualized recommendation rather than evidence that every GLP-1 has been proven to reduce birth control absorption." And if you're using an IUD, implant, patch or vaginal ring, this doesn't apply to you since they don't rely on digestion to work.

The "Ozempic babies" all over your Reels tell only part of the story. A 2025 study in PLOS One compared social media chatter about GLP-1 drugs and fertility with scientific literature and found a real gap: of 52 original studies on GLP-1 receptor agonists and fertility that turned up in a PubMed search, every single one was conducted in women with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, or PMOS (formerly polycystic ovary syndrome, or PCOS). Not one studied women without the condition.

That doesn't mean the excitement is baseless. It simply means it's specific.

"Women with PMOS have insulin resistance," explains Ikhena-Abel. That drives up testosterone and other androgens, disrupting communication between the brain and the ovaries. The result: follicles, "the small sacs where eggs develop, are arrested and unable to mature and release an egg," she says.

Weight loss, through GLP-1 use or otherwise, lowers insulin levels and can reverse that chain reaction. "Some patients experience more regular cycles and conceive naturally after starting GLP-1s due to more regular ovulation," Ressler says. In fact, in a 2017 randomized trial of 176 women with PMOS and excess weight, nearly 44% of those who took an older GLP-1 for 12 weeks got pregnant without fertility treatment, compared with about 19% of those who took metformin, a common diabetes drug often prescribed for PMOS. Still, Ressler cautions, "GLP-1s are not specifically fertility medications, and we cannot assume they will improve everyone's chances of pregnancy."

In short, GLP-1 drugs may help improve fertility by addressing some of the problems getting in the way.

Can GLP-1 drugs help if you don't have PMOS?

Outside of PMOS, the picture gets murkier. "There's a reason to think a GLP-1 could help some people who do not have PMOS, but it depends on why they are not ovulating," says Dr. Asima Ahmad , a reproductive endocrinologist in Chicago and chief medical officer of Carrot Fertility.

One common culprit: excess weight itself. Body fat produces estrogen, and too much of it can interfere with the hormone signals that tell your ovaries to mature and release an egg, Ahmad explains. As a result, ovulation may happen only sporadically or not at all, making it harder to get pregnant. Even modest weight loss can help: Doctors commonly recommend losing 5% to 10% of body weight for people whose fertility is affected by obesity, according to a 2026 review in Scientific Reports .

Ahmad points to a study that's nearly three decades old in which 60 of 67 women with obesity and infertility, across a range of diagnoses, resumed spontaneous ovulation after a structured weight loss program — no GLP-1 drugs involved. That study wasn't randomized, she notes, so she wouldn't promise the same result to everyone.

"The most important thing before any recommended treatment, whether that is weight loss or something else, is determining the cause of ovulatory dysfunction," Ahmad says. Irregular ovulation can also stem from thyroid disease , high prolactin, under-eating, overexercising, extreme stress, perimenopause or primary ovarian insufficiency, causes that a GLP-1 wouldn't necessarily address.

Perhaps. Research presented at the Endocrine Society's 2026 annual meeting suggests that testosterone levels and sperm parameters among men with obesity may improve with GLP-1 drugs. The caveats: The gains were clearest in men with low testosterone, and they mostly accompanied weight loss. "When healthy men without obesity were studied, no benefits were seen," Ikhena-Abel says.

Overall, the research on men remains "inconclusive," according to the 2026 JBRA review . In fact, in one case report, a man's sperm quality dropped with the older GLP-1 drug liraglutide (Victoza) and recovered after he stopped.

Either way, doctors say a male partner's prescription belongs in the fertility conversation. "Both partners' medications and medical histories are relevant when it comes to fertility," Ressler says.

Planning a pregnancy on a GLP-1? Here's what to do

If you're taking a GLP-1 drug and hoping to get pregnant, planning ahead matters: You generally "must discontinue use prior to pregnancy," Ressler says. "Animal studies have raised concerns about fetal growth, pregnancy loss and developmental abnormalities, while human data is still too limited to establish safety," Ahmad says. Plus, weight loss by any means isn't recommended during pregnancy, she adds. That's why the guidance is to stop before you start trying, not after a positive test. And because some of these drugs stay in the body for weeks, how far ahead you need to stop depends on which one you take:

*The labels for tirzepatide and liraglutide don't specify a preconception stop window. The tirzepatide range reflects guidance from Dr. Ilana Ressler and a 2026 review in JBRA Assisted Reproduction . The liraglutide window comes from the same review.

Sources: FDA labels for Ozempic , Wegovy , Rybelsus , Mounjaro , Saxenda and Foundayo ; MotherToBaby ; JBRA Assisted Reproduction ; Dr. Ilana Ressler

For men planning to become dads, the advice differs. "There's currently no established paternal stop window when it comes to GLP-1 use," Ahmad says. That doesn't mean it's been proven safe. There's simply little research on whether these drugs reach semen.

What if you get pregnant while taking a GLP-1?

"Don't panic," Ahmad says. She cites a 2026 analysis of more than 40,000 pregnancies exposed to GLP-1 drugs, which found no clear rise in birth defects. And in a separate 2026 study of 3,572 pregnancies in the Annals of Internal Medicine , people who kept taking a GLP-1 into early pregnancy didn't have a significantly higher risk of miscarriage. Their rates of major birth defects weren't significantly higher either, though the researchers say that finding is less certain.

Neither study proves these drugs are safe throughout pregnancy, but both are reassuring for the kind of accidental early exposure that's likely behind many of these headlines. Still, Ahmad says, you should stop GLP-1 use , call your prescriber and start prenatal care. If you have diabetes, you'll also need a plan to keep your blood sugar in check once you stop. And if you plan to breastfeed and resume GLP-1 postpartum, talk to your provider first: Ozempic's label notes that "it is not known if Ozempic passes into your breast milk."

GLP-1 drugs can affect fertility, but they're not fertility treatments. And don't skip backup birth control just because you think your odds are low. If you're on a GLP-1 and pregnancy is anywhere on your radar, whether you're trying for it or actively avoiding it, bring it up at your next appointment, not after the fact. "The key is individualized preconception planning rather than treating GLP-1 use and reproductive health as two separate conversations," Sekhon says.

Lucky Sekhon , MD, board-certified reproductive endocrinologist, infertility specialist and ob-gyn, and assistant clinical professor at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai

Ilana Ressler , MD, board-certified ob-gyn and reproductive endocrinologist at Illume Fertility in Norwalk, Conn.

Asima Ahmad , MD, board-certified ob-gyn and reproductive endocrinologist, and chief medical officer of Carrot Fertility

articles.title: Is Going to an Office Really Better for Your Health Than Remote Work? What the Research Shows
articles.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic changed the way we work.
articles.body: The COVID-19 pandemic changed the way we work. As the novel coronavirus spread, offices scrambled to move online. By mid-2020, the world had ushered in a new era of remote working. Employees traded commutes and cubicles for dining table desks, and business casual for loungewear. Coworkers adapted to virtual meetings, which pets and children often interrupted. The “new normal” of working remotely seemingly came with a host of benefits: better work-life balance, more flexibility, no stressful commutes and higher productivity. As COVID restrictions were lifted, some employers kept their remote work policies in place. Others shifted to a hybrid model, allowing employees to blend their work-from-home schedule with several days of in-office work each week. In recent years, many companies have changed tune, enforcing strict return-to-office mandates requiring employees work from the office four to five days a week. The justification? Bolster office culture and in-person collaboration. These mandates have been met with some pushback, with employees citing stress and burnout. A 2025 study from researchers at Harvard found that workers are willing to take a salary cut of up to 20% to have the flexibility to work remotely. Today, the work-from-home versus return-to-office debate remains polarizing. But personal preferences aside, what does the science show about the impact on wellbeing? Which practice is healthier for employees? Here’s what we know. Working Remote: Isolating or Empowering? A recent large-scale study suggests that working remotely — despite its popularity — may take a mental toll. The findings, published in June 2026 in Science, analyzed data from surveys of of 588,322 Americans spanning over a decade. “There’s a lot of evidence that people like working remotely; 80% of people think that it would be better for their mental health to work remotely at least some of the time,” Emma Harrington, Ph.D., an assistant professor of economics at the University of Virginia and co-author of the study, tells TODAY.com. The researchers compared post-pandemic changes in mental health among people who work “remotable” jobs, such as software engineering or marketing, to those who work “nonremotable jobs,” such as nurses or mechanics. The study drew on surveys spanning from 2011-2024, excluding the peak lockdown years of 2020-2021. They found that fully remote workers spent more hours alone and had less after-work socializing than in-person workers. “In people with remotable occupations, we saw a 50% increase in spending all day alone in the home and a 72% increase in the likelihood of not being in any ‘ambient contact’ with anyone all day, like, not anyone in the grocery store, truly isolated,” Natalia Emanuel, Ph.D., an economist and co-author of the study, tells TODAY.com. Simultaneously, workers in remotable jobs reported increased psychological distress. Researchers observed a 58% rise in mental healthcare visits and a 21% jump in prescriptions for antidepressants among fully remote workers, Emanuel notes. Remote workers who live alone saw the most dramatic impacts. “These (costs) are especially concentrated among people who were not living with a partner or kids,” says Emanuel. The findings were observational, meaning they do not prove that remote work causes poor mental health. However, the authors argue that the costs of remote work can be silent and build up for years. “The toll of isolation takes a while, it’s not an immediate impact on mental health. And it can be hard to differentiate what’s coming from remote work versus other changes in life, like a breakup, a new job or getting older,” says Harrington. The study did not examine other benefits of working remotely, such as skipping commutes or flexibility with childcare. “It’s not saying that remote work has no advantages. It’s saying for the average person, the costs of fewer in-person connections may outweigh the benefits,” says Harrington. Other research suggests the opposite. A study published this July in Frontiers of Psychology challenges the association between remote work and poor health. Researchers found that remote employees reported the highest level of wellbeing, while in-person employees reported the lowest in an analysis of 7,700 employees at a US healthcare company. Nicholas Bloom, Ph.D., an economics professor at Stanford University who has been studying the impacts of remote work for over 20 years, warns against the jumping to the conclusion that remote work worsens mental health. “For some people, it’s a godsend,” Bloom tells TODAY.com. “A large (proportion) of people will say being fully remote is best for their mental and physical health. They tend to be people in their 30s and 40s with long commutes and kids,” Bloom adds. Many people find remote work less stressful, Bloom says, and that it allows more time for exercise and other healthy habits. There’s some evidence that remote workers consume more home-cooked meals, contributing to healthier eating patterns — and they may have lower blood pressure, per a 2024 study. A 2025 review suggests that the flexibility of telework may reduce the amount of time taken off due to illness, facilitate a faster return to work and shorten the duration of sick leave. Remote Work and Accessibility For disabled and chronically ill people, the ability to work remotely is often a necessity, Imani Barbarin, a disability rights advocate who runs the blog Crutches and Spice, tells TODAY.com. “A staggeringly small number of disabled people are employed. There are people that do want to get into the office with disabilities, they just can’t,” Barbarin explains. Remote work reduces barriers. “It means more accessibility to get to doctor’s appointments, familiarity with their own space and not having to ‘perform’ in an office,” says Barbarin. Many disabled people benefitted from the rise of fully remote work during the pandemic. Return-to-office mandates and commuting present major challenges. Working remotely is a reasonable accommodation under the Americans with Disabilities Act, but employers aren’t obliged to grant this if it causes undue hardship or expenses. “When you’re working from home, you don’t have to deal with everyone else’s ableism or asking for accommodations, (and) the fear that this presents you as a lesser worker,” says Barbarin. However, Barbarin points out that flexible policies can benefit everyone in the workplace. “Remote work is accessibility that anybody can take advantage of. It promotes work-life balance, it allows for family time, and it allows people to work on their own schedule,” Barbarin says. The Return-to-Office Paradox Office work does have benefits. It can increase social interactions, get people out of the house, and create boundaries between work and home life, the experts note. “Some people want to go in every day. They feel working from home is not good for their health, or they find it isolating or depressing,” says Bloom. Social isolation is linked to a greater likelihood of mental illness, chronic disease and cognitive decline, per the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — young adults, such as those who entered the workforce after the pandemic, may be at higher risk. In addition to work-related interactions, the office facilitates casual connections with colleagues. “There’s evidence that that the office is the No. 1 place that American adults form new friendships,” says Harrington. But the experts emphasize that RTO mandates do not guarantee employees will see or speak to each other. “I find it sad when RTO mandates don’t coordinate workers, so on the day you go in, your team isn’t there or meetings are still happening over Zoom,” says Emanuel. “It makes your commute feel worthless because you’re just Zooming with different background.” Some research suggests people who work in an office have more physical movement and higher step counts, whereas working remotely increases sedentary behavior. However, Emanuel warns that office workers can still fall into the trap of sitting at a desk all day. “The value of the office is the opportunity to have face-to-face connection, both planned and spontaneous, (like) when you’re both getting coffee. If you never get out of your seat, you’re losing a lot of that benefit,” Emanuel says. It’s also on companies to ensure the workplace is conducive to employees’ wellbeing, the experts say. This means having comfortable seating, adjustable desks, natural lighting and good air quality — plus some employee perks. Accessibility and inclusion should also be a priority. “You can’t have you can’t have it both ways. You can’t demand people get into an office and then make that office inaccessible to them,” says Barbarin. WFH vs. RTO: Which Is Healthier? Remote work and office jobs both have benefits and downsides. Ultimately, the healthiest option depends on the individual and their needs, the experts emphasize. “The biggest lesson from all of this is choice. People are different, there really is no one size fits all,” says Bloom. Moderation is key, he adds. That’s why many experts argue that hybrid or flexible policies offer the best of both worlds. “The real sweet spot is having a situation where people can choose when they want to be in office,” Bloom says. Forcing people to return to the office full-time may not be the most productive strategy for employees or companies. In a landmark study on working-from-home professionals published in Nature in 2024, researchers found that employees who work one to two days from home per week were just as satisfied and productive as their in-office peers — plus, they were less likely to quit. “People know what’s best for themselves. ... On the managerial side, they can always figure out how check-ins and reporting are supposed to work,” Bloom adds. Tips to Stay Healthy At Work Whether you’re fully remote, in the office five days a week or somewhere in between, you can take steps to protect your health while working. First, avoid staying too sedentary. If you sit at a desk all day, try to get up and move your body at least once an hour. When you can, take the stairs or walk while taking calls. Try to prioritize quality sleep, nutrition and hydration during the workweek. And if you’re sick, stay home. Even if you don’t want to socialize at the office, it usually benefits people to make the most of their in-person time with colleagues, according to Harrington and Emanuel, who co-authored the upcoming book, “IN PERSON: How Working Together Fuels Creativity, Productivity, and Growth.” “To the extent possible, try putting yourself out there. ... Ask someone to get lunch with you, or linger at the coffee machine and strike up a conversation. Those little things can be helpful in making the most of the office,” says Harrington. Hate your commute? Reframe it as an investment. “You’re doing an unpleasant thing, but to get to a place where you can talk to other people and flex your social skills,” says Emanuel. Plan fun after-work activities near the office, like shopping or happy hour, to incentivize yourself to come in. Harrington suggests managers find ways to connect both in-office and remote employees, such as planning quarterly off-sites. If you’re fully remote, the experts suggest trying to combat isolation, especially if you live alone. “Make sure you leave the house, get some sunshine and walk around, have social contact outside of your household,” says Emanuel. Avoid over-working or pushing through the workday when you’re sick. Happiness impacts your health, too. If you’re miserable at work no matter the setting, it may be time to consider a job change.

articles.title: One type of sleep linked to dramatically lower risk of dementia, Parkinson's and 81 other diseases
articles.summary: Greater REM sleep was linked to 80% lower Parkinson's risk and 46% lower dementia risk in a major study of over 95,000 adults tracked for years.
articles.body: Not all stages of sleep are equal in terms of benefits for the brain. Greater amounts of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep were associated with lower risks of 83 diseases, including dementia, Parkinson’s disease and heart failure, new research has shown. Additionally, greater amounts of deep sleep were associated with lower risks of seven conditions. THIS ONE QUESTION MAY REVEAL WHETHER YOUR BODY IS GETTING THE REST IT NEEDS, STUDY FINDS That’s according to a study of 95,559 adults who wore wrist accelerometers continuously for seven consecutive days and nights. Researchers in China used deep-learning algorithms to analyze REM sleep, deep sleep, light sleep, total sleep duration, wakefulness after sleep onset and sleep irregularity. They then looked at health records to assess associations with more than 1,000 diseases over a nearly nine-year follow-up period. Greater REM sleep was associated with a significantly lower risk of several diseases, including Parkinson’s (80% lower relative risk), dementia (46% lower risk) and heart failure (26% lower risk). Greater deep sleep was associated with lower risks of seven conditions, including Type 2 diabetes and major depressive disorder. MORE NAPS, HIGHER RISK? RESEARCH LINKS DAYTIME SLEEP TO HEALTH WARNINGS IN AGING ADULTS Sleep duration was also found to be highly linked to disease outcome. Six to eight hours per night was found to be the "sweet spot" associated with the lowest risk for 69 diseases. In contrast, sleeping fewer than five hours per night was linked to an increased risk of 37 health conditions. The study also found that greater night-to-night sleep irregularity and more wakefulness during the night were associated with higher risks of several conditions, including anxiety and substance use disorders. The findings were published Sept. 17 in the journal PLOS Medicine. "I think what is important is the total duration of sleep, and the percentage that REM takes up," Oki Ishikawa, M.D., pulmonary, critical care and sleep medicine expert at Northwell’s Northern Westchester Hospital, told Fox News Digital. "The average percentage of REM sleep in this study population was about 20%, and generally 20-25% is considered normal per sleep cycle." 5-STEP SLEEP RESET COULD PROMOTE HEALTHY WEIGHT LOSS, NUTRITIONIST SAYS Ishikawa, who was not involved in the study, said he does not believe that a higher amount of REM sleep alone will necessarily lower the risk. "Normal sleep pattern and duration are associated with aspects like maintenance of good immune function and memory, so I think the important message here is to try and get a sufficient amount of sleep in general," Ishikawa sai. Disrupted sleep may sometimes be an early warning sign of disease rather than simply a cause, according to Dr. Chelsie Rohrscheib, head sleep expert at Wesper, a sleep analysis company in New York. "Conditions such as Parkinson’s disease, dementia and heart failure can begin affecting sleep years before they are diagnosed," Rohrscheib, who also was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital. "At the same time, poor sleep may contribute to disease progression, so the relationship likely works both ways." DIETITIAN REVEALS SIMPLE EATING STRATEGY FOR BETTER SLEEP — AND ONE HABIT TO AVOID The researchers noted some limitations of the study. Because it was observational, it could only show an association and could not prove that increasing REM or deep sleep directly prevents disease. "Sleep was measured for only one week using a wrist device, which is less accurate than a clinical sleep study for identifying sleep stages," Rohrscheib said. "Some health information was collected years earlier, medications that can affect sleep were not fully considered and some medical diagnoses may have been missed." As the participants were all from the UK Biobank, the study population was also less diverse and generally healthier than the overall population, so the findings may not apply equally to everyone, Rohrscheib noted. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "Overall, changes in sleep may provide important clues about underlying health, but this study cannot determine whether poor sleep is a cause, an early symptom or both," she concluded. Rohrscheib also cautioned that while wrist-worn sleep trackers are generally good at estimating sleep stages, they are not 100% accurate. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "Without a formal in-lab sleep study, it's impossible to know how much time the participants spent in REM and other sleep stages," she said. More research is needed to determine whether increasing REM or deep sleep can help prevent certain diseases, the researchers said. "If you get about seven to nine hours of uninterrupted sleep, you most likely have the opportunity to cycle through REM in a sufficient way." Future studies could also explore whether the relationship between sleep stages and disease risk varies by age, sex, overall health and other individual characteristics. Both experts recommended following general sleep hygiene practices, such as maintaining an optimal environment (dark, cool and quiet), keeping a consistent sleep schedule and avoiding sleep-disrupting substances such as alcohol and caffeine. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "If you have other sleep pathologies like sleep apnea … treating that would be a great way to optimize the amount of REM sleep," Ishikawa advised. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ While it can be difficult to measure REM sleep without a wearable, he said the best gauge is whether one feels refreshed upon waking and doesn’t feel sleepy during the day. "If you get about seven to nine hours of uninterrupted sleep, you most likely have the opportunity to cycle through REM in a sufficient way."

articles.title: Psychiatrist Reveals 9 Subtle Symptoms of Depression She’d Watch for in Herself
articles.summary: What are the symptoms of depression? A psychiatrist reveals the subtle warning signs she’d monitor in herself such as rumination, irritation and self-neglect.
articles.body: Depression can be insidious, affecting people in different ways with warning signs that aren’t always obvious. “Sometimes you are the last to know,” Dr. Samantha Boardman, a New York City psychiatrist, tells TODAY.com. “The people around you, the people who you spend time with are the ones who are aware of it before you are.” Almost 1 in 5 U.S. adults, 19%, say they currently have depression or are being treated for it, a rate hovering near the historical high, Gallup reported. Depression rates have “risen dramatically” among younger adults, it noted. Feeling sad for two weeks or longer to the point where it interferes with everyday life is a major symptom, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But there can be more subtle warning signs of depression, Boardman says. She practices positive psychology, which focuses on optimism, resilience and post-traumatic growth. “It’s really looking at those other questions — not just what’s wrong, but what’s strong?” says Boardman, who helps people find wellness within mental illness. “What is somebody’s strength? Tell me about a time you were at your best. How can you do more of that? Kind of getting people out of their heads rather than that self-focus and self-immersion that I think sometimes modern therapy is very focused on.” When it comes to depression, Boardman doesn’t want people to start over-diagnosing themselves. There’s a difference between sadness and a depressive episode, she emphasizes. There are also different types of depression. It’s important to look for a cluster of symptoms and a marked change from a person’s normal behavior, rather than making a quick diagnosis based on a little snapshot of a day, she cautions. “One has to be very careful about quickly putting a label on something and saying, ‘This is who I am, this is what I have,’” Boardman says. Knowing what she knows, here are the subtle symptoms of depression the psychiatrist would monitor in herself: Change in Appetite This could mean eating more or eating less than usual. “Am I forgetting about food?” Boardman might ask herself. Change in Sleep Patterns Sleeping more or sleeping less could both be signs of depression. “Usually, I sleep eight hours a night, no problem, and for the past months, I can’t get to sleep or I’m staying in bed. I just feel like lounging in bed all day. I feel like bed rotting,” the doctor says. Lack of Interest in Things You Used to Enjoy The loss of pleasure in activities that once brought joy is known as anhedonia. “Somebody (might) say, ‘Do you want to go to a concert? I’ve got tickets for Harry Styles,’ and you love Harry Styles, but you just don’t feel like it,” Boardman says. “Because it’s the absence of something rather than the addition of something, it’s sort of a hard thing to notice. That’s sometimes where friends or loved ones will notice that in you.” Social Withdrawal Are you pulling away from friends and family, or canceling plans? Boardman calls this a “huge” warning sign. Irritation Feeling frustrated, irritated, agitated or easily on edge can be a clue. Having a Hard Time Concentrating “I have five emails to return at work, and it takes me usually 10 minutes to do that. It’s taking me an hour,” Boardman says. Self-Neglect If somebody who typically likes to present herself in a certain way to the world is suddenly not doing that, it could be a warning sign. An example is a person who has always found it important to have beautifully coiffed hair and manicured nails, but is now showing up with unwashed hair or chipped nails. “There’s a change in their presentation in the world,” Boardman notes. Poor Posture The psychiatrist sometimes sees patients holding themselves differently, describing it as “folding in” on themselves. People with depressive symptoms can have a slumped posture, studies have found. They may also slow down, like they’re “moving through molasses,” or speak more slowly or with a softer voice, Boardman says. Rumination This means dwelling on negative thoughts and feelings, and replaying them on a loop, according to the American Psychiatric Association. It can be an “on ramp to depression,” Boardman warns. “You find yourself just rehashing, rehashing, rehashing something,” the doctor notes. “You get sort of stuck. … Why did this happen? What’s going on? Why am I feeling this way?” Best Self-Help for Depression Depression can be treated with therapy and medication. But there are also simple but powerful antidotes to the milder form of depression known as dysthymia, the psychiatrist says. “When this sort of does sneak up on you, the response is to shut down, to withdraw, to cancel your plans,” Boardman says. “We often hear: Be yourself … (but) this is exactly where you need to do the very opposite of the thing that you feel like doing.” Walk The easiest way to improve mental health is to go for a walk, preferably outside because nature is calming and a powerful stress reducer, so it can provide a reset button, the doctor notes. “Even when I don’t feel like it, when it’s pouring with rain, I walk,” Boardman says. “We know that being outdoors is great. Movement outdoors is even better. Movement outdoors with somebody else even better.” Do Something for Someone Else Boardman sometimes prescribes volunteer work for patients. “It’s a powerful way to not only distract but to give you that sense of agency — that you have a certain control over something and that you’re contributing to something beyond yourself,” she says. Practice Self-Distancing Instead of self-focus and self-immersion, give yourself some perspective. Boardman suggests asking yourself: What advice would I give to a friend in this moment?What would I think about the situation a month or two from now? How would a fly on the wall describe this? Depression is episodic — it comes and it goes, Boardman says, pointing to a quote poet Robert Lowell once wrote in a letter to a friend: “Life swims back.” If you’re severely depressed and need immediate help, call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

articles.title: South Carolina fitness trainer's cause of death made public as coroner defends husband
articles.summary: Elena Moore's autopsy revealed cardiac dysrhythmia with premature ventricular contractions, and her husband Brannon Slice was never a suspect.
articles.body: Nearly four months after the body of a missing South Carolina fitness enthusiast was found, authorities have determined that 39-year-old Elena Katherine Moore died of natural causes stemming from a heart condition, ending months of speculation surrounding her disappearance. Lexington County Coroner Margaret Fisher announced Friday that Moore died from complications of cardiac dysrhythmia with premature ventricular contractions, a condition involving an abnormal heart rhythm. Fisher said the autopsy found no evidence of traumatic injuries, including broken bones, strangulation or sexual assault. Toxicology testing detected alcohol but no other substances. SOUTH CAROLINA FITNESS TRAINER’S AUTOPSY RAISES MORE QUESTIONS ABOUT MYSTERIOUS DEATH "We never saw anything that would indicate homicide. Nothing," Fisher said. "We were able to follow her path. We were able to pull her medical history, her mental history. We knew that this was not a homicide." The coroner also addressed speculation surrounding Moore's husband, Brannon Slice, saying he was never considered a suspect or person of interest in the investigation. SOUTH CAROLINA FITNESS TRAINER TOLD FRIENDS SHE WANTED TO LEAVE HER NOW-HUSBAND YEARS BEFORE BODY WAS FOUND Fisher went further, crediting Slice with repeatedly trying to get his wife help as she struggled with a serious mental health crisis in the days before her disappearance. "The only person that really tried to help this girl to get her help through the system is her husband," Fisher said. "He reached out. He tried many times to get her help." SLED JOINS PROBE AS BODY MATCHING MISSING SOUTH CAROLINA PERSONAL TRAINER'S DESCRIPTION FOUND Moore was found dead June 17, six days after disappearing following her release from a mental health facility. articles.title: At 61 Years Old, This Grandmother of 12 Broke Her Own World Record With a 5-Hour Plank
articles.summary: A 61-year-old grandmother from Canada has wowed the internet by breaking her own Guinness World Record for longest time planking after holding the position for five hours.
articles.body: A 61-year-old grandmother from Canada has wowed the internet by breaking her own Guinness World Record for longest time planking after holding the position for five hours. DonnaJean Wilde of Welling, Alberta, helped kick off the Oct. 6 opening ceremonies at the Huntsman World Senior Games in St. George, Utah, when she planked in front of a crowd to beat her 2024 world record, for females, of 4 hours, 30 minutes and 11 seconds. Viral videos from the games, which celebrate athletes ages 50 and over, show Wilde planking on a platform with a smile on her face. One video has racked up more than 9 million views with commenters expressing their awe over Wilde’s feat. “I feel really good about it,” Wilde tells TODAY.com about her new world record. “Now that it’s done, I’m really happy.” The retired schoolteacher said she’d wondered for a long time if she could plank for five hours straight. She began training six months ago by planking between four and five hours every day. On Tuesday, she began her record-breaking plank with confidence, but shortly after she surpassed her record 2024 time, she began losing steam. “That last half hour was harder than I ever thought it would be, I think I just kind of hit a wall,” Wilde says. It was the crowd chanting her name that helped her get the job done. “The crowd was cheering through the last few minutes and they carried me through,” she says. “And now I look back and I think, ‘Wow, wow, we did it. We did it together.’” A Lifelong Love of Sports and Fitness The mom of five, who also holds a second Guinness World Record for most pushups in one hour by a female — she did 1575 of them in just under 60 minutes in 2024 — tells TODAY.com she fell in love with sports and fitness as a child. A lifelong runner, Wilde ran track in junior high and high school. She began planking 15 years ago after breaking her wrist in a gym accident. “I had a cast on and I couldn’t run. I couldn’t work out. I couldn’t do everything I wanted to do, and then I discovered planking,” Wilde recalls. At first, Wilde could hold the position only for a minute or two. She figured she’d keep at it until her cast came off and then return to her regular exercises. Instead, she “fell in love” with planking. “I just kept doing it and doing it ... so I planned my school lessons and marked my students’ work while I was planking,” says Wilde. For years now, Wilde has planked for about two hours every day, incorporating the low-impact exercise into other tasks. “I go on the floor and plank when I have something I need to do, like texting, emailing, reading or messaging somebody,” Wilde says, adding she also planks while doing an assignment or calling one of her kids. If Wilde’s husband Randy, 63, also a fitness enthusiast, turns on a movie, Wilde will watch it with him while on the floor planking. The physical benefits of planking can’t be beat. Planking helps tone all of the muscle groups, including abs, arms, back, shoulders, glutes and legs, experts say. Planking can also help improve balance, ease back pain and reduce belly fat. “Planking makes me feel so good and helps me stand up straight,” says Wilde. Asked how strong her core muscles are, Wilde simply laughs. The Kids and Grandkids Stay Fit, Too Wilde and her husband stay healthy by walking or running together every day. They also work out in their home gym. The couple’s kids and 12 grandkids have inherited their love of sports and fitness. “Ten out of 12 grandchildren at this moment are on at least one or two sports teams, like volleyball, basketball, baseball, football. The two who aren’t on sports teams are into dancing and gymnastics,” Wilde says. As for Wilde’s diet, she shares that she and Randy try to stick to fresh whole foods. “Lots of eggs, lots of real protein, lots of real fruits and vegetables, oatmeal, just real food,” Wilde says. “If we go somewhere, of course, then we will eat whatever anybody serves us. We don’t worry about it,” she adds. Does Wilde foresee herself attempting to break her world record for planking again in the future? “I’m not sure I’m going to try and break my planking record. Maybe my push-up record,” Wilde says, laughing.

articles.title: WVU collabs with Big 12 to host Women’s Empowerment Luncheon
articles.summary: West Virginia University, in collaboration with the Big 12, hosted a Women’s Empowerment Luncheon Friday at the Hope Coliseum in Morgantown, allowing student...
articles.body:
MORGANTOWN, W.Va. (WBOY) — West Virginia University, in collaboration with the Big 12, hosted a Women's Empowerment Luncheon Friday at the Hope Coliseum in Morgantown, allowing student-athletes and others to collaborate with community leaders.

The event, part of the Big 12's Fall Tour, travels across the U.S., bringing together community professionals, WVU students, athletes and university staff to hear from a panel of women leaders, including Amy Bush, President of WVU Medicine Golisano Children's Hospital.

Event organizers said that allowing young women to confide in community leaders and ask questions about their potential career paths is essential to building strong connections that can extend far beyond Morgantown.

"In this community, it's always great to elevate female voices and for young women in the community to be able to network with our leaders, for them to be able to see a path," WVU Athletics Marketing Representative Erin Gipson said.

The Big 12 Fall Tour also stopped at Mylan Park Elementary yesterday, giving students and teachers a classroom makeover ahead of the rest of the fall semester.

The next stop on the tour is Brigham Young University in Provo, Utah.

articles.title: Idosa questiona atuação de equipe médica que operou joelho errado | G1
articles.standfirst: Abalada, Marilda da Silva, de 72 anos, voltou ao hospital onde a cirurgia foi feita para receber acompanhamento de outro médico e desabafou: "não poderia ter acontecido".
articles.summary: Abalada, Marilda da Silva, de 72 anos, voltou ao hospital onde a cirurgia foi feita para receber acompanhamento de outro médico e desabafou: "não poderia ter acontecido".
articles.body:
Marilda da Silva, de 72 anos, voltou ao Hospital da Cruz Vermelha de Curitiba , nesta sexta-feira (9), para começar um acompanhamento após ter uma prótese implantada no joelho errado. Abalada, ela questionou a atuação da equipe médica que realizou o procedimento, em entrevista para a RPC, afiliada da TV Globo.

"Eu espero que seja feita justiça, para que não aconteça com outras pessoas o que aconteceu comigo. Porque isso aí é muito marcante, é uma coisa que não poderia ter acontecido. É uma equipe médica que está ali na sala de cirurgia, como que todo mundo errou?", desabafou ela.

A cirurgia foi realizada no dia 30 de setembro, após a realização de exames e o registro de documentos de que o joelho esquerdo passaria por uma artroplastia.

🔍A artroplastia é um procedimento que consiste em colocar uma prótese de metal e polietileno em superfícies ósseas e de cartilagens que estejam desgastadas.

"Quando eu sentei na mesa de cirurgia, eu ainda falei: 'é a perna esquerda', porque eles não marcaram, né? 'É a perna esquerda!'. Mas, mesmo assim, eles fizeram na perna direita. Depois eu só lembro que eu pus a minha mão e vi que eles tinham operado errado. Daí eu gritei com eles, eu falei 'vocês fizeram a cirurgia errada, meu Deus do céu, o que é isso?'. E ela [pessoa da equipe médica do hospital] falou 'calma, dona Marilda, tá tudo bem, a sua família já tá sabendo, tá tudo certo'", explicou a paciente.

Marilda da Silva ficou abalada ao retornar ao hospital após implante de prótese no joelho errado — Foto: Foto: RPC

O caso repercutiu após a filha de Marilda, Sabrina da Silva, fazer um relato nas redes sociais. Segundo ela, o médico ainda tentou culpar a paciente, dizendo que ela que havia pedido a troca . Entenda abaixo.

Idosa tem prótese implantada no joelho errado, em hospital particular de Curitiba

De acordo com Sabrina, a mãe estava com dificuldades para andar por conta de uma astrose no joelho esquerdo. Ela passou por exames e avaliações e o convênio liberou a cirurgia no joelho esquerdo. Porém, quando a paciente acordou da sedação, percebeu que o joelho direito que havia sido operado.

Sabrina relata que, ao questionar o médico que realizou o procedimento, ele disse que Marilda, já sob o efeito de medicamentos sedativos, havia insistido que o joelho direito tinha que ser operado, e que ele acatou o pedido da idosa.

"Ele me falou que a minha mãe, sedada, quando ela estava com sedação, ela foi muito insistente e ela quis mudar o joelho na hora ali. E segundo ele, isso é comum acontecer, e se o paciente quer trocar eles trocam ali na hora, não tem protocolo a seguir", contou Sabrina. "Não é o paciente que deveria decidir isso, não são os familiares, é o médico, nesta hierarquia, ele é o responsável, ele que comanda a cirurgia", disse em vídeo publicado nas redes sociais.

Idosa Marilda da Silva se recupera de operação no joelho errado, em Curitiba — Foto: Fotos: cedidas pela família ao g1/Arquivo Pessoal

Conselho Regional de Medicina apura o caso

O Conselho Regional de Medicina do Paraná (CRM-PR) afirmou em nota que acompanha o caso e que abriu uma sindicância para verificar a conduta da equipe responsável pelo procedimento. Disse ainda que, caso comprovada violação das regras éticas, as punições podem ir de uma advertência à cassação do registro profissional. Veja a íntegra da nota abaixo:

"O Conselho Regional de Medicina do Paraná (CRM-PR) informa que está acompanhando o caso e que instaurou processo de sindicância para apurar o ocorrido. Caso comprovada conduta violadora das regras éticas, as sanções previstas na Lei de criação dos Conselhos de Medicina vão desde advertência confidencial, podendo chegar à cassação do exercício profissional, a depender do grau de culpa e da gravidade das consequências apuradas.

Conforme estabelece o Código de Processo Ético-Profissional (Resolução CFM nº 2.306/2022), as sindicâncias e os processos ético-profissionais tramitam sob sigilo processual, garantindo às partes envolvidas os direitos constitucionais ao contraditório e à ampla defesa."

Idosa de 72 anos teve joelho errado operado em hospital particular de Curitiba. — Foto: Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Procurado pelo g1 , o Hospital Cruz Vermelha de Curitiba disse, em nota, que iniciou uma apuração interna para esclarecer o ocorrido e analisar os registros dos procedimentos adotados. Diz ainda que está programando a continuidade do acompanhamento da paciente por um médico ortopedista da equipe. Veja abaixo a íntegra:

"O Hospital Cruz Vermelha do Paraná informa que, ao tomar conhecimento dos fatos relatados pelos familiares da paciente, iniciou imediatamente uma apuração interna, com o objetivo de esclarecer as circunstâncias envolvidas, mediante análise técnica dos registros assistenciais e dos procedimentos adotados.

A instituição acompanhou a alta hospitalar e a evolução inicial da paciente, mantendo contato com seus familiares e adotando as providências necessárias à continuidade da assistência".
